rows: Extravaginal causes – urinary or rectal bleeding
Abnormal placental separation and other rare causes

items.text: Placenta praevia: Placenta partially or completely covers the internal cervical os. Classically causes painless, bright-red bleeding.
Abruptio placentae: Premature separation of a normally situated placenta. Typically painful bleeding, uterine tenderness and increased uterine tone.
Vasa praevia: Fetal vessels traverse the membranes over or near the cervical os. Rupture can cause severe fetal haemorrhage.
Local lesions: Cervical polyps, cervical cancer, vaginal trauma and infections.
APH is traditionally defined as bleeding from or into the genital tract after 24 weeks of pregnancy and before delivery.
Never perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound.
Maternal haemodynamic stability does not guarantee fetal wellbeing.

rows: Cervical, vaginal and perineal tears; uterine rupture

items.text: Tone: The commonest cause. The uterus fails to contract effectively after delivery.
Trauma: Bleeding from genital tract injuries despite a well-contracted uterus.
Tissue: Retained placental tissue prevents effective uterine contraction.
Thrombin: Failure of the coagulation system to form stable clots.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: A soft, boggy uterus suggests atony. A firm uterus with persistent bleeding should prompt a search for genital tract trauma, retained tissue or coagulopathy.
Primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours after delivery.

rows: Obstructed or prolonged labour-related uterine exhaustion
Non-delivery or retention of placental tissue

items.text: Uterine overdistension – multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, macrosomia.
Uterine exhaustion – prolonged or precipitate labour.
Uterine-relaxing drugs – magnesium sulphate, beta-agonists and certain anaesthetic agents.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Primary PPH is an obstetric emergency. Management involves simultaneous resuscitation, identifying the cause, uterotonics, tranexamic acid when indicated, and escalation to mechanical or surgical haemostasis.
Secondary PPH occurs after the first 24 hours and up to 12 weeks postpartum in the commonly used contemporary definition.

items.text: Retained products of conception are an important cause.
Endometritis causes fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia.
Subinvolution of the placental site causes persistent or recurrent bleeding.
Gestational trophoblastic disease should be considered when bleeding persists with abnormal β-hCG.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Secondary PPH is often associated with retained tissue or uterine infection. Ultrasound and clinical assessment help guide investigation and management.
Remember the major direct and indirect causes.

items.text: Diabetes and other pre-existing medical disorders.

blocks.title: Examination pearl: Maternal deaths are commonly classified into:

items.text: Direct obstetric deaths – resulting from obstetric complications, interventions or omissions.
Indirect obstetric deaths – resulting from pre-existing or newly developed medical conditions aggravated by pregnancy.

blocks.text: This is a useful emergency resuscitation framework, supplemented by obstetric-specific causes.

items.text: T – Toxicity from drugs or magnesium sulphate.

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: Call for help, assess airway and breathing, obtain circulation access, initiate resuscitation and investigate the underlying cause simultaneously. In cardiac arrest during pregnancy, use left uterine displacement and follow the pregnancy-specific resuscitation protocol.
Pre-eclampsia is not caused by a single identifiable disease. It is a multifactorial placental and maternal vascular disorder.

items.text: Inadequate trophoblastic invasion of maternal spiral arteries.
Spiral arteries remain relatively narrow and high-resistance.
Reduced placental perfusion and placental ischaemia.
Release of antiangiogenic and inflammatory factors.
Vasoconstriction, hypertension, proteinuria and end-organ injury.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Pre-eclampsia usually develops after 20 weeks of gestation. It is diagnosed by new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or other maternal organ dysfunction; proteinuria is not mandatory.
Eclampsia is the occurrence of new-onset generalised seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, not explained by another cause.
Important pearl: Eclampsia can occur before, during or after delivery, including postpartum.

items.text: C – Cerebral complications: stroke, seizures, cerebral oedema.
S – Stillbirth and fetal growth restriction.
H – Hepatic complications: haematoma or rupture.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: HELLP syndrome is a severe manifestation of pre-eclampsia, but it may occur without the classic degree of hypertension or proteinuria.
Preterm labour refers to labour occurring before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy.

rows: Maternal smoking, malnutrition and other risk factors

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Preterm labour is not synonymous with preterm birth. True labour involves regular uterine contractions associated with progressive cervical change.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Causes of premature rupture of membranes (PROM)

blocks.text: PROM is rupture of membranes before the onset of labour. When this occurs before 37 weeks, it is called preterm PROM (PPROM).

items.text: R – Previous PROM or preterm birth.
A – Abnormal cervical anatomy or cervical insufficiency.
N – Nutritional deficiencies and poor maternal health.
E – Excessive membrane stress and weakening.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Major complications include ascending infection, cord prolapse, placental abruption, prematurity and pulmonary hypoplasia in very early prolonged PPROM.

rows: Hypotonic uterine contractions, inadequate expulsive effort
Contracted pelvis, pelvic tumour, cervical obstruction

items.text: Powers: Inadequate frequency, duration or strength of contractions.
Passenger: Occiput posterior position, brow presentation, transverse lie, fetal macrosomia.
Passage: Cephalopelvic disproportion, pelvic deformity, soft tissue obstruction.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Prolonged labour and obstructed labour are not interchangeable. Prolonged labour may occur without absolute mechanical obstruction.

items.text: Failure of cervical dilatation or descent.

blocks.text: The preferred clinical term is suspected fetal compromise.

items.text: X – eXcessive cord compression or prolapse.
A – Anaemia in fetus or maternal hypoxia.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: An abnormal CTG is not itself a diagnosis. Interpret the baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations in clinical context.

rows: Other maternal disease – renal, cardiac, autoimmune
Reduced placental function or structural abnormalities

items.text: Congenital infections, including CMV, toxoplasmosis, rubella and syphilis.
Symmetrical growth restriction: head, abdomen and length are proportionately affected; often associated with early fetal or genetic causes.
Asymmetrical growth restriction: abdomen is disproportionately small relative to head circumference; often associated with placental insufficiency.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Fetal growth restriction is not the same as a constitutionally small fetus. Growth trajectory, estimated fetal weight, abdominal circumference and Doppler findings help distinguish them.

items.text: T – Thrombophilia and placental vascular disorders.
H – Hypoxia and fetal growth restriction.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Evaluation may include maternal history, placental examination, fetal examination or autopsy when appropriate, and targeted laboratory investigations.

items.text: O – Obstructive fetal urinary tract abnormalities.
F – Fetal renal agenesis or dysplasia.
D – Drugs: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs.
Pulmonary hypoplasia when severe and early.
Limb contractures in prolonged severe cases.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Oligohydramnios is commonly defined using ultrasound as a single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm or an amniotic fluid index of 5 cm or less, depending on the method used.

items.text: C – Congenital infections and fetal anaemia.

blocks.text: Recurrent pregnancy loss is commonly defined as two or more pregnancy losses in some contemporary guidelines; older definitions frequently use three consecutive losses. Always specify the guideline being used.

items.text: Chromosomal: parental balanced translocations, embryonic aneuploidy.
Hormonal: uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an important treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.text: T – Tubal damage from previous infection.
U – Use of assisted reproductive technology.
A – Abnormal tubal anatomy or surgery.
L – Lifestyle-related risk factors, particularly smoking.
Conception with an intrauterine contraceptive device in situ.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Classic triad: amenorrhoea, abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. However, not all patients present with all three.

items.text: R – Renal or systemic maternal illness.

blocks.text: Most common cause: Chromosomal abnormalities of the embryo, particularly in early pregnancy loss.
Examination pearl: The presence of vaginal bleeding with a closed cervical os and a viable intrauterine pregnancy is characteristic of threatened miscarriage.

items.text: E – Episiotomy or perineal wound infection.
R – Retained placenta and manual removal.
L – Caesarean section and surgical wound infection.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Puerperal sepsis can progress rapidly to septic shock. Start appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, obtain cultures where this does not delay treatment, and achieve source control.

rows: Wound – caesarean or perineal wound infection

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Do not automatically attribute postpartum fever to endometritis. Examine the breasts, abdomen, wounds, urinary system and lower limbs.

items.text: T – Thyroid dysfunction or other medical illness.
R – Relapse of schizophrenia or affective illness.
Sudden onset, often within the first two weeks postpartum.

blocks.text: Postpartum psychosis is different from postpartum blues and postpartum depression.

items.text: Baby blues: mild, transient emotional symptoms.
Postpartum psychosis: severe illness with possible delusions, hallucinations and risk of harm.

blocks.text: Urgent psychiatric assessment and hospital-level care are required. The mother and baby need an immediate safety assessment.

rows: Onset of established labour to full cervical dilatation
Full dilatation to delivery of the baby
Delivery of baby to delivery of placenta and membranes

items.text: Latent phase: Cervical effacement and early dilatation.
Active phase: Progressive cervical dilatation. The exact threshold differs between guidelines; WHO uses 5 cm for active labour, while some other guidelines use 4–6 cm.
Passive second stage: Full dilatation before active pushing.
Active second stage: Full dilatation with involuntary or active pushing and descent.
Active management: Prophylactic uterotonic, controlled cord traction where appropriate.
Physiological management: Spontaneous placental delivery without routine intervention.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: The third stage ends with delivery of the placenta and membranes, not the delivery of the baby.
The mechanism of labour describes the sequence of fetal movements through the maternal pelvis during vaginal birth.

rows: Fetal head moves down through the pelvis
Biparietal diameter passes the pelvic inlet
Chin approaches chest, presenting smaller diameter
Occiput rotates anteriorly, usually towards symphysis pubis
Head extends beneath the pubic arch and is delivered
Head rotates to align with shoulders

blocks.text: Important clarification: Descent is continuous and engagement may occur before labour, particularly in multiparous women. Some textbooks arrange these movements differently or combine restitution with external rotation.
Examination pearl: The mechanism described above applies to normal vertex, occipito-anterior delivery. Malpositions and malpresentations have different mechanisms.

items.text: Engagement: Biparietal diameter passes through the pelvic inlet.
Descent: Head progresses down the birth canal.
Flexion: Fetal chin approaches the chest, presenting the suboccipitobregmatic diameter.
Internal rotation: Occiput rotates anteriorly towards the pubic symphysis.
Extension: Head extends and emerges beneath the pubic arch.
Restitution: Head rotates to realign with the shoulders.
External rotation: Shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior pelvic diameter, and the head follows.

blocks.text: The mechanisms of labour and cardinal movements describe substantially the same process, but textbooks may divide or combine the movements differently.

rows: Assessment of maternal and fetal health

items.text: Fundal height and fetal lie later in pregnancy.
Urinalysis and urine culture as indicated.
Tetanus-containing vaccination according to immunisation history.
Aspirin prophylaxis for eligible women at increased risk of pre-eclampsia.

blocks.title: WHO recommends a minimum of eight antenatal contacts:

blocks.text: Examination pearl: ANC is not simply routine visits. It includes prevention, early diagnosis, treatment, risk assessment and preparation for safe delivery.
Examination pearl: Stabilisation of the mother is the priority in most obstetric emergencies. Maternal resuscitation often provides the best opportunity for fetal survival.

rows: Eclampsia or severe maternal disease when delivery is indicated and vaginal birth is unsuitable
Previous uterine surgery with contraindication to labour

items.text: Placenta praevia covering the internal cervical os.
Cord prolapse when immediate vaginal birth is not feasible.
Elective caesarean section – planned before labour.
Emergency caesarean section – undertaken urgently because of maternal or fetal indications.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Caesarean section should be based on clinical indication and informed consent. Not every breech presentation, previous caesarean or case of fetal compromise automatically requires the same approach.

items.text: Increased risk of placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum in future pregnancies.
Uterine scar rupture in subsequent pregnancy.
Respiratory morbidity, particularly with elective early-term delivery.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Caesarean delivery is major abdominal surgery. Its risks extend beyond the immediate postoperative period to subsequent pregnancies.

rows: Cardiac assessment of fetal heart rate
Cardiac assessment of fetal heart rate

items.text: Fetal movement counting – maternal perception of fetal movements.
Intermittent auscultation – Pinard stethoscope or handheld Doppler.
CTG – evaluates fetal heart rate and uterine contractions.
Ultrasound – fetal growth, anatomy, placental location and liquor volume.
Doppler velocimetry – assesses blood flow, particularly umbilical artery and middle cerebral artery.
Biophysical profile – fetal breathing, movements, tone, amniotic fluid and NST.
Non-stress test – assesses fetal heart rate accelerations in response to movement.

blocks.text: Examination pearl: Surveillance methods should be selected according to maternal risk factors, gestational age and the clinical question. An abnormal result requires clinical interpretation and an appropriate response.

items.text: Repeated every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes if the 5-minute score is below 7.
It assesses the newborn's clinical condition and response to transition and resuscitation.
It is not a predictor of an individual child's long-term neurological outcome.
Do not delay neonatal resuscitation to complete APGAR scoring.
A low score should prompt assessment and appropriate support, not substitute for clinical judgement.

blocks.text: The Bishop score evaluates cervical favourability before induction of labour.
Examination pearl: A favourable cervix is more likely to respond to induction. An unfavourable cervix may require cervical ripening with appropriate prostaglandins or mechanical methods.
A partograph (or partogram) is a graphical tool used to monitor labour progress and maternal-fetal wellbeing.

items.text: Urinary protein and ketones where indicated.
Alert line: Traditionally represents expected cervical dilatation progress.
Action line: Traditionally positioned four hours to the right of the alert line in the classic WHO partograph.

blocks.text: If labour progress crosses the alert line, reassessment is required. Crossing the action line historically prompted consideration of intervention after evaluation.

Important modern update: WHO's Labour Care Guide replaces the rigid expectation of 1 cm/hour cervical dilatation with evidence-based assessment of labour progress and individualised clinical decision-making. The classic partograph remains important for examinations, but should not be used as an automatic indication for caesarean section.

items.text: Identify the chart and time scale.
Review maternal pulse, BP and temperature.
State the diagnosis and recommend appropriate action.
